transcript.text:
"Stopped working" can mean a few different things with a vacuum, and the cause depends on which. - No power getting to it: the socket, the fuse in the plug, a damaged cable, or on a cordless, a flat or failing battery or charger.
Most vacuums switch themselves off if the motor overheats, usually because a blockage or a clogged filter has starved it of air. It then stays dead until it cools down.
• It runs but won't pick up: a full bin or bag, a blocked hose or wand, or filters clogged with fine dust.
• The brush bar has stopped spinning because of hair wrapped round it or a snapped drive belt. These checks should sort it out, simplest first. 1. Plug a lamp or phone charger into the same socket. If that doesn't work, the socket or the house circuit is the problem. If a corded vacuum is still dead in a socket you know works, look along the cable for damage. Then try checking the plug fuse with one of the rating marked on the plug. A fuse that blows again straight away points to a fault inside the vacuum, so stop using it.
2. Empty the bin or fit a new bag. Take out the filters, tap them clean, and wash them only if the manual says they're washable (let them dry fully, at least 24 hours). Look through the hose and wand for anything stuck. 3. After clearing any blockage, leave it unplugged for an hour or so to cool, then try again. If it now runs, the cut-out was the cause, and keeping the filters and hose clear should stop it happening again.
4. On a cordless, put it on charge and check the charging light comes on. If it charges but dies within seconds, the battery is the likely culprit.
5. Turn the floor head over and cut away any hair or thread wound round the brush bar, then check it turns freely by hand. If it's still completely dead after all that, with a known-good socket and fuse, the likely culprits are the switch, an internal wire or the motor. That needs a closer look rather than more home checks. To point you in the right direction: is it corded or cordless, and when you switch it on is it completely dead, or does the motor run but it won't pick up (or the brush won't spin)?
its corded, the red Henry one. completely dead when I switch it on, no motor at all. the lamp works in the same socket

That's useful. The problem is between the plug and the motor. A motor that's simply worn out usually gives some warning first, such as cutting in and out, sparking or a burning smell, rather than going dead with no warning. 1. Unplug it and put a new 13A fuse in the plug, or borrow one from another plug that you know works. If Henry then runs, it was the fuse. If the new fuse blows again straight away, stop using it, because that points to a fault inside.
2. With it unplugged, run the whole cable through your hands. Look and feel for cuts, flattened sections, kinks or exposed inner wires. Pay most attention to the first few inches by the plug and where the cable goes into the machine. Henry cables get wound round the top and pulled a lot, so those are the usual places for a hidden break. Any damage means the cable needs replacing, so don't use it until then.
3. If it stopped mid-clean, it's worth one more try after it has been switched off and unplugged for an hour, with the hose and filter checked for blockages, just to rule out overheating. If the fuse is good and the cable looks fine, the next suspects are the on/off switch or the motor's carbon brushes. Checking either means opening up the head. Henrys are very repairable and parts are easy to get, so a vacuum repair shop or engineer can usually sort it for much less than a new one. That's the better route unless you're confident working on mains appliances. Have you swapped the plug fuse yet, and does the cable look intact along its length?

I haven't got a screwdriver or a spare fuse. There's some black tape on the cable near the plug, my son did it ages ago, and it's a bit bent there. Once it came on for a second when I moved the wire but I'm not doing that again, it frightened me.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Stop using it now. If you can do it safely, switch it off at the socket or at the consumer unit (fuse box). A shock usually means an earth or insulation fault, so don't use it again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has found and fixed it. Please leave Henry unplugged and don't use it again until it's been repaired. The socket works. There's an old tape repair near the plug with a bend at that spot, and it came on for a moment when the wire moved. That pattern is a classic broken wire inside the cable at the damaged point. The wires inside are only touching now and then, which is why it's dead most of the time and flickers when moved. I'm fairly confident that's the fault, so swapping the fuse isn't worth chasing now. 1. Don't re-tape it or try to wiggle it back into life. Tape isn't a safe repair on a mains cable, and a part-broken wire can overheat or leave live metal exposed.
2. Once it's unplugged, it's fine to wrap the cable loosely and leave it alone so nobody else picks it up and tries it.
3. A vacuum repair shop or an appliance engineer should check the cable and plug and fit a proper replacement cable. It's a very routine job on a Henry. They'll also make sure nothing else was damaged by the faulty connection. On cost, Henrys are built to be repaired. A new cable is usually a modest bill compared with a new vacuum, so repair is probably worth it, as long as the motor is otherwise healthy. Many local repair shops will do it while you wait or within a day or two.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
